chunk_findings.detail: The recovery code is moved into the `ddflow.services.leases` package, but the deferred completion import in `_note_landed` still uses `__package__` to build the module name. In the old top-level `ddflow/services/leases.py`, `__package__` was `ddflow.services`, so `importlib.import_module(f"{__package__}.completion")` imported `ddflow.services.completion`. In `ddflow/services/leases/recovery.py`, the same expression names `ddflow.services.leases.completion`, which is not part of this change and does not exist. Running `ddflow recover` (or any code path calling `scan`) over an expired lease whose worktree is clean and whose merge commit is on the base reaches `_note_landed`, executes that import, and raises `ModuleNotFoundError` instead of returning the completion advice. The import must target the parent service package explicitly (for example `ddflow.services.completion` or `importlib.import_module(".completion", package="ddflow.services")`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/recovery.py:_note_landed

chunk_findings.detail: The lazy re-export table omits `lapsed_onto_a_live_claim`, even though the manifest states that `ddflow/services/leases/lifecycle.py` adds that name. Because `__getattr__` only resolves names listed in `_SUBMODULE_OF`, `from ddflow.services.leases import lapsed_onto_a_live_claim` or `ddflow.services.leases.lapsed_onto_a_live_claim` hits the `sub is None` branch and raises `AttributeError`; `dir(ddflow.services.leases)` also omits it. This breaks the stated “public API unchanged” invariant for a public, non-underscore lifecycle helper.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/__init__.py:60-72 (_SUBMODULE_OF lifecycle block)

chunk_findings.detail: The live-holder early return bypasses the glob/resource conflict checks even when the re-claim changes those fields. If item A is held live by agent H with no globs, and item B is held live by another agent with globs covering `src/x.py`, then H calling `acquire(log, cfg, "A", holder=H, globs=["src/x.py"])` reaches the `existing.live(...) and existing.holder == holder` branch, calls `_record_claimed_globs` and `_renew_in_place`, and returns before the later `glob_clash` / `_break_idle` block. The renewed lease for A now covers `src/x.py`, creating two live claims over the same file. The same path skips the resource-capacity check, so `--resources gpu:8` on a live own lease can also overcommit when another live lease already holds the capacity.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/claim.py:_acquire_locked

chunk_findings.detail: `_renew_in_place` records a new note in the `lease.renewed` event (`if note: upd["note"] = note`) but never assigns it to the mutated `Lease` object. For example, re-claiming your own live lease with `note="new"` logs the new note, while the `Lease` object returned by `acquire` (and the in-memory `existing`) still reports the old `note`. The returned public lease object is therefore inconsistent with the event log.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/claim.py:_renew_in_place

chunk_findings.detail: In `_live_pairs`, when the held glob `b` contains a wildcard, the pair is kept if any changed path matches the requested glob `a`; it does not require that changed path to also be covered by the held glob `b`. Given the same release line and no shared globs, suppose another item has an active wildcard lease `src/*` and its worktree has changed only `tests/x.py`, while the caller requests `*/*`. `conflicts` returns the pair `('*/*', 'src/*')` because both globs match `src/y.py`; `holder_changed_paths` returns `['tests/x.py']`; `GL.match('tests/x.py', '*/*')` is true, so `_live_pairs` keeps the pair and `_clash_text` drops/refuses `*/*`. But `src/*` does not cover `tests/x.py`, so the wildcard lease has no real changed work overlapping `*/*`; the claim should not be refused. The wildcard case should require a changed path to match both `a` and `b` (or at least `b`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/common.py:_live_pairs

chunk_findings.detail: `_same_clone` treats an absent current clone id as matching every named clone: `return not (theirs and clone and theirs != clone)` is true whenever `clone` is empty, although the docstring only says a claim without a clone is this clone's. `lost_contests` calls `log.clone_id(create=False)` (line 106), which can return an empty/`None` id in a repository or clone that has not created a clone id. Given a log containing an acquisition for item `X` with `data={"holder": "alice", "clone": "other-clone"}` and a later `lease.released` for `X` with `data={"holder": "alice", "lost_contest": True, "event": <acquisition id>}`, `_ours` (line 94) returns true because the current clone id is empty, so `lost_contests` reports item `X` as a contest this clone lost. The function's own contract says a release of another clone's claim under the same name is not ours; a caller using the returned winner/branch will act on another clone's lost contest.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/contests.py:88 (_same_clone)

chunk_findings.detail: `renew` mutates the local log before it checks the remote claim. It first calls `_transition(...)`, which appends a `lease.renewed` event when the local lease is mine and not quieted, and only afterwards returns `not _remote_renew(...)`. The comment immediately above that return says that if the remote claim was taken over, the lease “is not renewed” and the function should return `False`. Given remote claims enabled and a remote claim already held by another holder, this input makes the function append a local renewal (unless the renewal was quieted) and then report failure: the fold now shows the lease extended/renewed while the caller is told the renewal did not happen. If `_remote_renew` uses the opposite boolean convention, the same ordering is still wrong because the local append happens before any remote decision.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/lifecycle.py:renew

chunk_findings.detail: The dataclass declares `salvageable: bool | None = False` immediately after saying `False` means *measured clean* and `None` means *could not measure*, and warns that collapsing unknown into clean lets `sweep(apply=True)` remove unmeasurable trees. But because the field has a default, any valid construction that omits `salvageable`—e.g. `Recovery(item="i", holder="h", kind="orphan_worktree", worktree="/tmp/w")`—produces `salvageable is False`, which the flag's own semantics interpret as a completed measurement showing the tree is clean. If a recovery path cannot measure the worktree and fails to pass `salvageable=None` (or if a new caller omits it), `sweep(apply=True)` will treat it as safe to remove. The default should be `None` (or the field should be required) to preserve the three-valued invariant.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/model.py:43 (Recovery.salvageable)

chunk_findings.detail: `scan` classifies an expired lease whose worktree is clean and fully merged as `salvageable=False`, and then `_note_landed` rewrites the advice to say the item must be completed, not released (explicitly citing Ba2eff5726b). `sweep(apply=True)` still only checks `rec.kind == "expired_lease" and rec.salvageable is False`, so for a non-terminal, non-adopted item whose merge gate passed and whose `merged_sha` is reachable from the base, it calls `expire(log, rec.item, ...)`. That clears/expires the claim instead of completing the item, returning it to the queue to be claimed/merged again—the exact behavior the comment says is wrong. The sweep path should skip or mark unsweepable the recoveries that `_note_landed` identifies as landed-on-base.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/recovery.py:sweep

chunk_findings.detail: When `dispose_finished` is called for an item whose worktree directory is already gone, it delegates to `_drop_branch`. `_drop_branch` re-reads protection with `_protected(root, cfg, localize(fold(log.read_all(), strict=False), log, time.time()))`, but it does not pass `ignore=item.id`. That differs from `dispose_tree`, whose documented behavior is that the caller’s own live lease does not count. Concrete input: the caller is `merge`, item `I` still has a live lease held by this caller, `I.worktree` no longer exists on disk, and `I.branch` exists and is fully merged into the base. `dispose_finished(..., it=I)` calls `_drop_branch`, `_drop_branch` sees the branch as held by `I` itself, and returns `(False, "")`; the branch is silently kept even though the same caller would have been allowed to dispose of the tree/branch through `dispose_tree`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup/dispose.py:_drop_branch

chunk_findings.detail: `sweep_finished` treats an item with no known finish time as old whenever `cfg.worktree.sweep_min_age_s == 0`, contradicting its own contract that “an item with no known finish time is never old.” The code computes `finished_for = CK.age_s(stamp, now) if stamp else 0.0`, then only skips when `finished_for < cfg.worktree.sweep_min_age_s`. With `sweep_min_age_s=0`, a DONE item with empty `completed_at` (or a terminal item with no recorded `item.abandoned`/`task.removed`/`phase.removed` stamp) gets `finished_for=0.0`; `0.0 < 0` is false, so the sweep proceeds and may remove the item’s leftover worktree. The guard should skip when `stamp` is empty, or use a strict “older than” check that does not treat age 0 as elapsed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup/dispose.py:sweep_finished

chunk_findings.detail: The lazy re-export only repairs the attribute being looked up. Because the submodules `survey` and `apply` have the same names as public callables, any import of those submodules lets Python’s import machinery bind the package attribute to the module object, bypassing `__getattr__`. For example, `from ddflow.services import cleanup as CL; import ddflow.services.cleanup.apply; CL.apply` returns the module `ddflow.services.cleanup.apply`, not the `apply` function, so `CL.apply(...)` raises `TypeError: 'module' object is not callable`. The same can happen for `survey`, including through sibling imports such as `from .survey import ...` in another submodule, so the public API is not unchanged and late-bound monkeypatch-sensitive names can be silently replaced by module objects.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup/__init__.py:75-90

chunk_findings.detail: The package has no `__all__`, so `from ddflow.services.cleanup import *` does not import the public cleanup API. Star-importing uses the package’s actual module namespace (or `__all__` if present) and does not call `__getattr__` for names listed only in `_SUBMODULE_OF`; the added `__dir__` does not affect star imports. Thus code like `from ddflow.services.cleanup import *; dispose_tree(...)` gets `NameError: name 'dispose_tree' is not defined`, whereas the old single-file module would have exposed `dispose_tree` through star import.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup/__init__.py:__dir__

chunk_findings.detail: The change is supposed to preserve monkeypatch-sensitive names via late binding, but `apply.py` binds `Path` at import time (`from pathlib import Path`) and then uses that module-local binding directly in `_registered`, `_pruned_scratch`, and `_remove_planned`. In the original single-module `cleanup.py`, monkeypatching `ddflow.services.cleanup.Path` changed all path operations used by these functions. After the split, a test or caller that patches the package attribute (e.g. `ddflow.services.cleanup.Path`) still causes `apply.py` to use the real `pathlib.Path`, so `_pruned_scratch` can still evaluate `Path(t.path).exists()` / `_registered(...)` against the real filesystem and report success/failure contrary to the patched environment. This violates the stated no-behavior-change/late-binding requirement for the preserved API.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup/apply.py:13

chunk_findings.detail: The module imports `Path` from `pathlib` at module scope and uses it at runtime in `stands_in` (`Path(where).resolve()`) and in `sweep_finished` (`Path.cwd()`). The stated split contract requires preserving monkeypatch-sensitive names, including `Path`, via late binding. In the original single module, patching `ddflow.services.cleanup.Path` changed those uses; after this split, patching the package attribute does not change `dispose.py`'s own module-level `Path`. For example, a test or caller that monkeypatches `cleanup.Path` to make `Path.cwd()` return a finished worktree's directory would expect `sweep_finished` to keep that tree, but this module still calls the real `pathlib.Path.cwd()` and may remove the tree.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup/dispose.py:12

chunk_findings.detail: The submodule binds `Path` directly into its own namespace (`from pathlib import Path`), so `_key` resolves `Path` from `ddflow.services.cleanup.model`, not from the historical public module path `ddflow.services.cleanup`. chunk_findings.detail: `reexport(globals(), ...)` leaves the imported `reexport` function in every package’s module dict, so the package namespace is no longer the same as before. Before this change, `hasattr(ddflow.services.ci, "reexport")` was false; after it, it is true, and `from ddflow.services.ci import *` (the shown `__init__.py` files do not define `__all__`) binds `reexport` to the helper. This violates the stated requirement that public/private name resolution be unchanged, and it will shadow any legitimate `reexport` name in a package or clobber a local `reexport` in a module that uses star-import from one of these packages.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/_reexport.py:reexport

chunk_findings.detail: The new `from ddflow.core._reexport import reexport` binds the public name `reexport` in the package namespace, and the visible `reexport(globals(), _SUBMODULE_OF, __name__)` call does not hide it (same pattern appears in configwrite/flow/review). Thus after `import ddflow.services.flow`, `hasattr(ddflow.services.flow, "reexport")` is true and `dir(ddflow.services.flow)` lists `reexport`, whereas before the change no such attribute existed. If the package has no `__all__`, `from ddflow.services.flow import *` now imports the helper and can shadow a caller's `reexport`, changing public/private name resolution contrary to the stated invariant.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/companions/__init__.py:36

chunk_findings.detail: The call site imports the helper as a public name (`from ddflow.core._reexport import reexport`), leaving `reexport` in the package module namespace. As a result, `dir(ddflow.services.upgrade_apply)` now includes `reexport`, and if the package has no `__all__`, `from ddflow.services.upgrade_apply import *` will bind `reexport` to the shared helper. Before the change that name was not present in the package namespace and would have gone through the lazy `__getattr__` path (raising `AttributeError` unless it was a `_SUBMODULE_OF` key). This changes public/private name resolution, which the intent explicitly says must remain unchanged. The same issue exists in `ddflow/views/markdown/__init__.py:101`; importing the helper as `_reexport` (e.g. `from ddflow.core import _reexport` and calling `_reexport.reexport(...)`) would avoid introducing a new public attribute.

chunk_findings.detail: `_TRAILING_CITE` only captures the *last* trailing bracket group, so a bullet that cites several lessons in separate trailing brackets is treated as citing one. Given a hand-written summary bullet like `- **Cache invalidation.** explanation [L12] [L13]`, `tail.group(1)` is `L13`, so `_summary_bullet` records `cites=["L13"]` instead of `["L12", "L13"]`. `_attach_summaries` then sees exactly one citation and, if lesson `L13` has no summary yet, attaches this bullet as `L13`'s summary instead of importing it as a consolidated rule; the citation to `L12` is lost. This misattributes summary provenance and can suppress the consolidated lesson the importer is supposed to create when a bullet cites more than one lesson.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_scan.py `_summary_bullet`

chunk_findings.detail: The namespace injection only publishes names listed in each submodule's `__all__`; it does not publish the core helpers imported by the package itself (`glob_match`, `_slug`, `_slug_words`). The file's comment says the flat namespace is published into each submodule so functions can call helpers by bare name, and the noqa imports of `_slug`/`_slug_words` indicate they are intended to remain in that flat namespace. Given a submodule function that uses one of these names bare (as the original flat module could), calling it through the package will raise `NameError` because the name is present in the package globals but absent from the submodule's globals; the `globals().update(_EXPORTS)` call does not inject it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/__init__.py:40

chunk_findings.detail: With `[dedupe] on_match = "warn"`, `_resolve_chains` is called unconditionally on the `dropped` map even though no duplicate is actually left out in warn mode. If a summary lesson `A` duplicates a non-summary lesson `B` from the same import (`where="import"`, score 1.0), and `B` duplicates an existing queue record `C` (`where="queue"`, score 0.8), `_resolve_chains` rewrites `A`'s duplicate to point at `C` (`of="C"`, `where="queue"`, `identical=False`, `score=0.8`). Since warn mode keeps `B` in `plan.found`, `A` should still be reported as duplicating `B` in this import; the code instead hides the exact in-import duplicate and reports a transitive `A ~ C` relation that `similar.screen` never established. This violates the function's own contract that a chain is resolved only when the intermediate record "is itself left out."
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_apply.py:_dedupe_found

chunk_findings.detail: `_triage_found` builds `closed` by appending `Found` objects (`closed.append(f)`), but `_note_withheld` is written for `closed: list[str]` and renders it with `', '.join(closed[:_NOTE_EXAMPLES])`. Given a source file that yields a closed/declined open task and `include_done=False`, `_triage_found` returns that item as a `Found` in `closed`; when the plan_import path passes the returned `closed` to `_note_withheld`, `str.join` raises `TypeError: sequence item 0: expected str instance, Found found`. The comment in `_note_withheld` explicitly says closed items should be named like held ones, so `_triage_found` should append an id/title string, not the `Found`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_phases.py:_note_withheld / _triage_found

chunk_findings.detail: Uniquifying against only `proposed` before checking `known` makes already-imported handling order-dependent. Suppose the queue already contains item id `L-x` from a prior import, and this scan contains two items whose scanner-derived id is also `L-x`: a new item first, then the already-imported item. The new item gets `L-x` from `_unique`, then the `f.ident in known` test treats it as the existing item and skips it. The already-imported item then gets uniquified to `L-x-2`, is no longer seen as known, and is appended to `plan.found`, duplicating the existing `L-x` item on re-run. If the second item has `legacy_ident=L-x`, it is instead skipped under the wrong suffixed id and the new item is never imported. `existing_phases` and `plan.skipped_existing` also receive the suffixed id, so phase settle later cannot match the queue item.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_phases.py:_triage_found

chunk_findings.detail: `_note_sources` strips the source string at the first colon before testing for the `git:` scheme: `rel = str(n["source"]).split(":", 1)[0]`, then `if rel and not rel.startswith("git:")`. For a note whose source is `git:feature-branch`, `rel` is `git`, and `"git".startswith("git:")` is false, so the function adds the path `git` to `paths`. `verify_import` later stats `repo / "git"`; in a normal repository with no regular file named `git`, it reports that imported note as having a vanished source. The intended exclusion of branch/git provenance never happens.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_plan.py:_note_sources

chunk_findings.detail: The empty-phase removal only treats phases as live when they are referenced by items already in `plan.found`: `live_phases` is built from `plan.found` tasks and `plan.found` needs. It ignores already-existing open queue items. If the folded queue contains an open task `T` whose `needs` includes phase id `P`, and this import proposes phase `P` but no tasks under `P` (for example, `T` was queued separately and only the phase is missing), `P` is classified as an empty phase and removed. The import then leaves `T` depending on an unknown phase, which is treated as unmet, while the proposal can report success; this is precisely the failure mode the added `needs` union comment says it was meant to avoid.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_cap_or_settle

chunk_findings.detail: The final “Nothing recognisable was found” note is added whenever `plan.found`, `plan.skipped_existing`, and `plan.duplicates` are all empty, even when items were recognised and deliberately withheld. For example, with a todo file containing one checked box and `include_done=False`, `_triage_found` defers the ticked item, `plan.ticked_left_out` becomes 1, `_note_withheld` records that history was left out, `plan.found` is empty, and the end-of-function condition still appends “Nothing recognisable was found.” The same false note appears after an over-cap refusal or after all phases are dropped as empty: the plan has notes explaining what it found and withheld, but the operator is also told nothing recognisable was found.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_plan.py:plan_import

chunk_findings.detail: When a summary bullet has no explanation after its bold lead, `_summary_text` returns the lead or stray punctuation instead of an empty summary. For input `- **Rule**` (body `**Rule**`) and target title `Rule`, `_LEAD` matches, `rest` is empty, `same` is true, and `return (rest or text) if same else text` returns `**Rule**`, so the lesson's summary duplicates its title. For `- **Rule.**`, the terminal period is not consumed because the separator requires following whitespace, so `rest` is `.` and the summary becomes `.`. This contradicts the function's stated purpose of removing the bold lead when it is the title.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_scan.py:_summary_text

chunk_findings.detail:
The table scanner treats any indented line as a table row because it tests `lines[i].lstrip().startswith("|")`. In Markdown, a line indented four spaces or more is an indented code block, not structure. Given a file containing:

```markdown
    | id | title |
    |----|-------|
    | T1 | Do not import |
```

`fenced[i]` is false (there is no ```/~~~ fence), and the `lstrip()` check accepts all three rows, so `_scan_task_tables` emits a `Found` task for `T1` from what is actually example code.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_tables.py:_scan_task_tables

chunk_findings.detail:
The scanner decides a line is a table header solely from “names id/title and next line is a delimiter”, without checking that the line is the first row of a GFM table. Consecutive pipe rows belong to one table, so a data row can be mistaken for a new header. Given:

```markdown
| name | value |
|------|-------|
| id | title |
|------|-------|
| T1 | Do |
```

a GFM renderer treats this as one table whose header is `name/value`, with `id/title`, `---`, and `T1/Do` as data rows. The code sees the third row as a header followed by a delimiter, sets `cols`, skips the delimiter, and then imports `T1` as a task from the supposed new table.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_tables.py:_scan_task_tables

chunk_findings.detail: `_disposition` returns closed for any checkbox text that merely starts with `~~`, but its own contract says a struck-through item is `~~...~~`. Given the raw item text `~~TODO` (no closing `~~`), the function returns `("closed", "STRUCK THROUGH")` and the live item is disposed as history, even though the tildes are literal/unbalanced rather than Markdown strikethrough.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_tables.py:_disposition

chunk_findings.detail: The negation regex has no word boundary after its short alternatives and places `no` before `nothing`, so it matches the `no` prefix inside ordinary words. In `_prose_needs`, this regex is matched against the text immediately after a dependency keyword. Given `text="Requires node and P2.T1"`, `known={"P2.T1"}`, and `self_id=""`, `_PROSE_NEGATING.match(" node and P2.T1")` succeeds because of the `no` in `node`, so `_prose_needs` returns `[]` instead of `["P2.T1"]`. The same defect defeats the intended `nothing but` exception: `Requires nothing but P2.T1` is also treated as negated and drops the dependency, which can make the importer emit a task without a required dependency and let the queue offer it too early.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_titles.py:_PROSE_NEGATING

chunk_findings.detail: `_box_disposition` cannot return an explicit ACTIVE disposition. The code and comments encode active as an empty first element (`("", "")`), but the function only returns inherited dispositions when `inherited[0]` is truthy. Thus an inherited `**STATUS**: ACTIVE` is treated as “no status.” In an archive file, the next line then applies the archive fallback. For example, in an archived file with heading `## Active work`, line `**STATUS**: ACTIVE`, and checkbox `- [ ] finish feature`, the stack entry is `("", "")`, `inherited[0]` is false, `archived` is true, and the function returns `("hold", "in an archive file ...")`. The task is imported as held despite the section explicitly saying ACTIVE, contradicting the function’s docstring and the stack comment that explicit ACTIVE overrides inheritance.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_todo.py:_box_disposition

data.consequences: A new split package must reuse the helper, not inline the boilerplate; the added import is private and del-ed to keep the monkeypatch contract.
data.context: The inline __getattr__/__dir__/_MODULES block was duplicated across 8 (now more) split packages and pylint duplicate-code counted it as an R0801 cluster, pushing the duplicate_code_clusters ratchet over baseline=1.
data.decision: Every one-file module split into a <30k package re-exports its public API through ONE shared ddflow/core/_reexport.reexport helper. The package imports it as the PRIVATE module name (from ddflow.core import _reexport), calls _reexport.reexport(globals(), _SUBMODULE_OF, __name__), then del _reexport, so neither the public name reexport nor the helper binding leaks into the package namespace and from-pkg-import-star and dir() are unchanged.
data.title: Split packages re-export lazily via a shared ddflow.core._reexport helper

data.summary: When a split package re-exports names via a shared helper, importing the helper as the PUBLIC name (from ddflow.core._reexport import reexport) leaves reexport as a new public attribute (import-star + dir() expose it). Import the helper MODULE as the private name and del _reexport after the call so the package namespace is byte-for-byte what it was.
data.title: A lazy re-export helper import must be private and del-ed after the call
data.why: see r-reuse-core and duplicate_code_clusters: the 8-copy inline block was an R0801 cluster; the helper import leaked a new public name.

chunk_findings.detail: The module declares ports in `ddflow.core.ports` and documents fakes under `tests/fakes`, directly contradicting the recorded operator decision D-adapters-answers-2, which requires ports to live next to their adapters in `ddflow/adapters` and fakes to live in shipped `ddflow/adapters/fakes`. The concrete failure is the documented adapter pattern: `ddflow/adapters/forge` is supposed to expose a `Registry[Forge]` keyed by `name`, so it must import `Forge` from `ddflow.core.ports`; that makes the bottom adapter layer import `ddflow.core`, violating the same file’s stated contract that `ddflow.adapters` imports no other ddflow layer while `core` may import adapters, and creating a layering cycle. If the import is avoided to preserve the layer contract, the ports are not “next to their adapters” as required, and the shipped `ddflow/adapters/fakes` package required by D-adapters-answers-2 cannot hold the fakes because this document routes them to `tests/fakes`. [D-adapters-answers-2]

chunk_findings.detail: The added adapters table says the default implementations under `ddflow/adapters` are “the default implementations of the ports in `core/ports.py`”, and the manifest confirms a new `ddflow/core/ports.py`. That contradicts [D-adapters-answers-2], which says ports (Protocols) live next to their adapters in `ddflow/adapters`, not in `core`. A developer following this documentation will place Protocols in `ddflow/core/ports.py`; because the same section declares `adapters` to be the bottom layer that imports no other ddflow layer, adapters then cannot import those port declarations to implement or register them without violating the stated layering, and the required “port lives next to its adapter” model is wrong.

The manifest confirms the implementation follows the wrong doc (`ddflow/core/ports.py` is a new file), so a default adapter such as `ddflow/adapters/proc` must import `ddflow.core.ports.Proc` to implement `Proc`, creating an upward `adapters -> core` dependency from the bottom layer and a cycle risk when `core.digest` re-exports an adapter; a ratchet looking for shipped fakes also finds none. chunk_findings.detail: The import guard misses plain imports of forbidden IO modules and relative imports into `ddflow`. For example, adding `import subprocess` to `ddflow/core/ports.py` passes because the `ast.Import` branch only flags names starting with `ddflow`; `subprocess` is only checked for `ImportFrom`. Likewise, adding `from . import adapters` or `from .adapters import X` passes because the relative import’s module top is `""` or `"adapters"`, not `"ddflow"`, even though it imports ddflow code from inside the ddflow package.

chunk_findings.detail: This test only inspects top-level module statements, so executable code inside `Protocol` class bodies is allowed. For example, `ddflow/core/ports.py` containing `class Proc(Protocol): def run(self, argv): return 42` passes the test, despite the test’s stated invariant that a port is declaration-only and that a port body is a second implementation. The guard therefore does not prevent implementations from being hidden inside port classes.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_class_code` guard still permits class-definition-time code hidden in signatures, so `test_ports_are_declarations_only` does not enforce “nothing runs.” It inspects method bodies, method/class decorators, and class bases, but it does not inspect method argument defaults (or annotation expressions). chunk_findings.detail: The `clock-env` family is mapped to the entire `os` root module, although the stated family is time/uuid/random/os.environ. Because `_external_roots` records only import roots, any module that does `import os` or `from os import path` for `os.path` is placed in `clock-env.importers`; since `clock-env` has no declared home, `FamilyReport.violations` lists it. For example, adding `ddflow/foo.py` containing `import os` and using `os.path.join("a", "b")` makes `ddflow.foo` a `clock-env` violation even though it never touches `os.environ`. This misclassifies ordinary path use as clock/env/randomness dependency and can make the ratchet baseline grow for code that should not belong to the `clock-env` family.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/archdeps.py:37

chunk_findings.detail: `_external_roots` swallows `SyntaxError` and `OSError` and returns no imports. A file that cannot be parsed or read is silently treated as having no dependencies, so a forbidden import in that file is invisible to the census. For example, create `ddflow/foo.py` containing `import subprocess` followed by a syntax error such as `def f(:`; `_external_roots` catches the `SyntaxError` and returns `()`, so `scan(repo)` reports no `subprocess` importer and no violation, allowing a new importer outside the family’s home to evade the ratchet. The census should fail or report the unparsable/unreadable file rather than omit it from the dependency census.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/archdeps.py:101-104

chunk_findings.detail: The command registers itself under `tool="ddflow_archdeps"`, i.e. a new tool named after the command, even though the stated intent and D-unify require this to be an action on the existing tool/view surface (consistent with `family="ddflow_view"` and `help_group="view"`). Loading `COMMANDS` therefore either fails registry validation against the existing tool set or creates a second tool; in either case the `archdeps` action is not added to the existing tool’s action surface, violating the strangler/ratchet requirement [D-unify].
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/arch_deps.py:22

chunk_findings.detail: The ratchet test cannot enforce “baseline ignore lists only shrink” because it compares the scan against the same editable `BASELINE` literal in the test file. Given a change that adds a new module outside a family’s declared home, e.g. `ddflow.foo` importing `sqlite3` outside `ddflow.infra.docindex`, and the same change appends `"ddflow.foo"` to `BASELINE["sqlite3"]`, `test_ratchet_violations_match_baseline` sees `got == want` and passes; `test_default_scan_reports_every_family` also passes because `"sqlite3"` is already in the family set, and `test_violations_are_importers_outside_the_home` still passes for `http`-style no-home families because violations equal importers. This contradicts the stated ratchet requirement that a new importer outside a home fails and that baselines only shrink.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_arch_deps.py:test_ratchet_violations_match_baseline

chunk_findings.detail: `_external_roots` promises to return `None` when a file “cannot be read or parsed,” but it only catches `OSError` and `SyntaxError`. A file that cannot be decoded as UTF-8 raises `UnicodeDecodeError` from `path.read_text`, and a file containing a null byte raises `ValueError` from `ast.parse`; neither is caught, so `scan` crashes instead of putting the module in `Census.unparsed`. For example, adding `ddflow/foo.py` with invalid UTF-8 bytes (or `b"\x00"`) makes the census fail outright rather than reporting the file as unparsed, contradicting the stated “never skipped” behavior and the ratchet’s need to know when dependency data is unavailable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/archdeps.py:_external_roots

chunk_findings.detail: The added `write_text` calls put unescaped newlines inside ordinary single-quoted string literals (e.g. `write_text("import subprocess` followed by a real line break and then `")`). This makes `tests/test_arch_deps.py` itself syntactically invalid: importing/collecting the test module raises `SyntaxError: unterminated string literal`, so the new test cannot run and the whole test file fails collection.

chunk_findings.detail: The module declares ports in `ddflow.core.ports` and documents fakes under `tests/fakes`, directly contradicting the recorded operator decision D-adapters-answers-2, which requires ports to live next to their adapters in `ddflow/adapters` and fakes to live in shipped `ddflow/adapters/fakes`. The concrete failure is the documented adapter pattern: `ddflow/adapters/forge` is supposed to expose a `Registry[Forge]` keyed by `name`, so it must import `Forge` from `ddflow.core.ports`; that makes the bottom adapter layer import `ddflow.core`, violating the same file’s stated contract that `ddflow.adapters` imports no other ddflow layer while `core` may import adapters, and creating a layering cycle. If the import is avoided to preserve the layer contract, the ports are not “next to their adapters” as required, and the shipped `ddflow/adapters/fakes` package required by D-adapters-answers-2 cannot hold the fakes because this document routes them to `tests/fakes`. [D-adapters-answers-2]
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/ports.py:10

chunk_findings.detail: The added adapters table says the default implementations under `ddflow/adapters` are “the default implementations of the ports in `core/ports.py`”, and the manifest confirms a new `ddflow/core/ports.py`. That contradicts [D-adapters-answers-2], which says ports (Protocols) live next to their adapters in `ddflow/adapters`, not in `core`. A developer following this documentation will place Protocols in `ddflow/core/ports.py`; because the same section declares `adapters` to be the bottom layer that imports no other ddflow layer, adapters then cannot import those port declarations to implement or register them without violating the stated layering, and the required “port lives next to its adapter” model is wrong.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:218

chunk_findings.detail: The ratchet paragraph documents today’s ignore-imports baseline as “8 `core -> config`”, but [D-adapters-answers] states that the reconciled layer contract folds in “9 `core->config`” baseline entries. If the actual `.importlinter` ratchet contains 9 entries, this documentation undercounts the shrink-only baseline and can mislead someone auditing or removing ignore entries; if it contains 8, the documented contract still does not match the stated decision data.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:192

chunk_findings.detail: The new “Adapter model” section documents ports as being declared in `core/ports.py` and fakes as living in `tests/fakes/`, contradicting D-adapters-answers-2, which says ports live next to their adapters in `ddflow/adapters` and fakes live in shipped `ddflow/adapters/fakes` with a ratchet requiring every port to have a fake. The manifest confirms the implementation follows the wrong doc (`ddflow/core/ports.py` is a new file), so a default adapter such as `ddflow/adapters/proc` must import `ddflow.core.ports.Proc` to implement `Proc`, creating an upward `adapters -> core` dependency from the bottom layer and a cycle risk when `core.digest` re-exports an adapter; a ratchet looking for shipped fakes also finds none. [D-adapters-answers-2]

chunk_findings.detail: The test pins the port module to `ddflow/core/ports.py` and imports `ddflow.core.ports` at collection time. The operator decision `D-adapters-answers-2` recorded in the context says ports live next to their adapters in `ddflow/adapters`, not in `core`. Therefore this guard enforces a forbidden layout: if the ports are moved to `ddflow/adapters/ports.py` as required, the test fails with an import/collection error; if `ddflow/core/ports.py` remains, the test is pinning the wrong architecture. It does not verify that any fake exists, does not verify that every declared port has a fake, and does not verify the shipped fake location required by `D-adapters-answers-2` (`ddflow/adapters/fakes`). With no fakes anywhere, the test passes, so the required “every port has a fake” ratchet is not enforced; with fakes in `ddflow/adapters/fakes`, the test also passes while its own docstring claims fakes are never shipped under `ddflow/`. chunk_findings.detail: The import guard misses plain imports of forbidden IO modules and relative imports into `ddflow`. For example, adding `import subprocess` to `ddflow/core/ports.py` passes because the `ast.Import` branch only flags names starting with `ddflow`; `subprocess` is only checked for `ImportFrom`. Likewise, adding `from . import adapters` or `from .adapters import X` passes because the relative import’s module top is `""` or `"adapters"`, not `"ddflow"`, even though it imports ddflow code from inside the ddflow package.

chunk_findings.detail: This test only inspects top-level module statements, so executable code inside `Protocol` class bodies is allowed. For example, `ddflow/core/ports.py` containing `class Proc(Protocol): def run(self, argv): return 42` passes the test, despite the test’s stated invariant that a port is declaration-only and that a port body is a second implementation. The guard therefore does not prevent implementations from being hidden inside port classes.

chunk_findings.detail: The guard still pins the port contract to `ddflow/core/ports.py`; the changed docstrings explicitly say `ddflow/core/ports.py`, and the test’s `PORTS_PATH`/import continue to target that module. [D-adapters-answers-2] records that ports live next to their adapters in `ddflow/adapters`, not in `core`. If a developer follows that operator decision and puts the Protocol in `ddflow/adapters/ports.py` (or removes `ddflow/core/ports.py`), this test fails at collection or when reading the missing `PORTS_PATH`, so the contract enforces the forbidden layout. chunk_findings.detail:
The new class-body check filters out only `ast.FunctionDef`, not `ast.AsyncFunctionDef`. Given a valid port declaration such as:

```python
from typing import Protocol

class Proc(Protocol):
    async def run(self, argv: list[str]) -> int: ...
```

the method body is only `...`, but `class_body` includes the `AsyncFunctionDef` node because `not isinstance(b, ast.FunctionDef)` is true for async methods; `_opaque` returns that node, and the assertion fails. Thus the guard rejects legitimate async Protocol methods.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ports_contract.py:`test_ports_are_declarations_only`

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_class_code` guard still permits class-definition-time code hidden in signatures, so `test_ports_are_declarations_only` does not enforce “nothing runs.” It inspects method bodies, method/class decorators, and class bases, but it does not inspect method argument defaults (or annotation expressions). For example, adding `class Proc(Protocol): def run(self, argv = exec("print('x')")) -> int: ...` to `ddflow/core/ports.py` leaves the method body as an ellipsis and the base/decorators clean, so `_class_code` returns no problems and the AST guard passes; importing the ports module evaluates the default argument and executes `print('x')`. Thus arbitrary code can be placed in a port’s default argument and bypass the declaration-only ratchet.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ports_contract.py:_class_code

chunk_findings.detail: The new default guard treats every non-`ast.Constant` default as “runs code”, which rejects legitimate signed literal defaults. For a valid port declaration such as `class Proc(Protocol): def run(self, timeout: int = -1) -> int: ...`, Python’s AST represents `-1` as `UnaryOp(op=USub(), operand=Constant(value=1))`, not as an `ast.Constant`. `_class_code` therefore emits “an argument default runs code” and `test_ports_are_declarations_only` fails, even though the default is a declaration and not a second implementation. The same over-rejection applies to other safe literal defaults such as `= ()` or `= {}` if those are intended to be allowed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ports_contract.py:96

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_literal` predicate accepts any unary operation on any literal, not just signed numeric literals. For example, a port method default written as `def run(self, x=-"") -> int: ...` parses as `UnaryOp(op=USub(), operand=Constant(value=""))`; `_literal` recurses to the string constant and returns `True`, so `_class_code` will not report `an argument default runs code`. That default is not a literal declaration (it is a unary expression evaluated at class-definition time, and in fact raises `TypeError`), so the declarations-only guard is overpermissive. The fix for `-1` should restrict the operand of `USub`/`UAdd`/`Invert` to numeric constants (or bool), not to any literal.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new class-body check filters out only `ast.FunctionDef`, not `ast.AsyncFunctionDef`. Given a valid port declaration such as:

```python
from typing import Protocol

class Proc(Protocol):
    async def run(self, argv: list[str]) -> int: ...
```

the method body is only `...`, but `class_body` includes the `AsyncFunctionDef` node because `not isinstance(b, ast.FunctionDef)` is true for async methods; `_opaque` returns that node, and the assertion fails. Thus the guard rejects legitimate async Protocol methods.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ports_contract.py:`test_ports_are_declarations_only`

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_class_code` guard still permits class-definition-time code hidden in signatures, so `test_ports_are_declarations_only` does not enforce “nothing runs.” It inspects method bodies, method/class decorators, and class bases, but it does not inspect method argument defaults (or annotation expressions). For example, adding `class Proc(Protocol): def run(self, argv = exec("print('x')")) -> int: ...` to `ddflow/core/ports.py` leaves the method body as an ellipsis and the base/decorators clean, so `_class_code` returns no problems and the AST guard passes; importing the ports module evaluates the default argument and executes `print('x')`. Thus arbitrary code can be placed in a port’s default argument and bypass the declaration-only ratchet.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ports_contract.py:_class_code

chunk_findings.detail: The new default guard treats every non-`ast.Constant` default as “runs code”, which rejects legitimate signed literal defaults. For a valid port declaration such as `class Proc(Protocol): def run(self, timeout: int = -1) -> int: ...`, Python’s AST represents `-1` as `UnaryOp(op=USub(), operand=Constant(value=1))`, not as an `ast.Constant`. `_class_code` therefore emits “an argument default runs code” and `test_ports_are_declarations_only` fails, even though the default is a declaration and not a second implementation. The same over-rejection applies to other safe literal defaults such as `= ()` or `= {}` if those are intended to be allowed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ports_contract.py:96

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_literal` predicate accepts any unary operation on any literal, not just signed numeric literals. For example, a port method default written as `def run(self, x=-"") -> int: ...` parses as `UnaryOp(op=USub(), operand=Constant(value=""))`; `_literal` recurses to the string constant and returns `True`, so `_class_code` will not report `an argument default runs code`. That default is not a literal declaration (it is a unary expression evaluated at class-definition time, and in fact raises `TypeError`), so the declarations-only guard is overpermissive. The fix for `-1` should restrict the operand of `USub`/`UAdd`/`Invert` to numeric constants (or bool), not to any literal.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ports_contract.py:_literal

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_literal` unary branch uses one operand-type rule for `USub`, `UAdd`, and `Invert`. `Invert` (`~`) is not valid for floats, so `~1.0` is not a signed numeric literal and is not a declaration. If a port contains `class Proc(Protocol): def run(self, x = ~1.0) -> int: ...`, `_literal` returns `True` because the operand is an `ast.Constant` with a `float` value, so `test_ports_are_declarations_only` passes even though the default is an invalid unary expression evaluated at function-definition time. This is the same class of false negative as the previously confirmed `-""` case; the fix should not treat `~float` as a literal declaration.

A file such as `ddflow/core/pathutil.py` containing `from os.path import join` is recorded as an importer of the `clock-env` family because `_external_roots()` returns `("os",)`, and `AstArchDepsCensus.scan` then adds that module to `stdlib_importers["clock-env"]`. Since `clock-env` has no declared home, `FamilyReport.violations` reports every importer as a violation. chunk_findings.detail: The package initializer imports `_Parsed`, `_Delta`, and `_MERGED` from `._parse`, but it does not import or re-export `_Merged`, which the change manifest explicitly says `_parse.py` adds. Since the old `ddflow.infra.log` module exposed `_Merged`, an unchanged call site such as `from ddflow.infra.log import _Merged` now raises `ImportError: cannot import name '_Merged'`. This breaks the stated no-behavior-change/unchanged-call-sites requirement.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log/__init__.py (import block from `._parse`)

chunk_findings.detail: The function’s own docstring says `DDFLOW_AGENT` overrides the derived identity, but the implementation never reads `os.environ` or `DDFLOW_AGENT`. Given `DDFLOW_AGENT=worker-1 default_agent_id(fallback_root=repo)`, the code returns `host-tree-suffix` instead of `worker-1`, so the documented escape hatch for multiple agents in one tree does not work.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log/_agent.py:default_agent_id

chunk_findings.detail: When `fallback_root` is omitted, `root` is `""`, so `_clone_suffix` is never called and the returned id has no clone suffix. In an adopted checkout, `default_agent_id()` therefore returns `host-<checkout>` instead of the documented `host-<checkout>-<clone-suffix>`. This can reintroduce the B190 cross-clone collision merely because the caller used the default argument.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log/_agent.py:default_agent_id

chunk_findings.detail: The initial `with contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError): return path.read_text("utf-8").strip()` is outside the later `try/except OSError`. If `.ddflow/local/clone-id` exists but is unreadable (for example after being restored with mode `000`), `read_text` raises `PermissionError`, which is not caught, so `default_agent_id` crashes instead of falling back to an unsuffixed or safe identity.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log/_agent.py:_clone_suffix

chunk_findings.detail: `_linked_tree_here` verifies only that a stored relative worktree path resolves to a linked worktree in this clone’s `git worktree list`; it cannot distinguish this clone from a teammate whose event records the same relative worktree string (e.g. both have `../feature`). If this clone’s `.ddflow/events` contains a merged teammate shard and the clone-id file is deleted, `_recovered_suffix` can adopt the teammate’s suffix and give this clone the same identity as that teammate.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log/_agent.py:_linked_tree_here/_recovered_suffix

chunk_findings.detail: `append_many` is documented as all-or-nothing, and specifically that "a reader never sees half of a merge or a split", but the code writes and `fsync`s each event one at a time while readers take no lock. A concurrent reader that reads the shard after the first `_write` returns but before the second starts will see only the first event, even when the second event later succeeds. The input is two valid kinds; process A pauses inside `append_many` between the two appends while process B calls `read_all` and observes the half-written unit.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log/_eventlog.py:append_many

chunk_findings.detail: The rollback path for a failed `append_many` only `os.truncate`s the current shard and restores `_lamport`; it does not undo the earlier `_meta.advance` and `APPEND_HOOKS` side effects made by an event that was already written before a later item raised. For `[("valid","s",{}), ("__no_such_kind__","s",{})]`, the first event has already been passed to `services.shardmarks` high-water-mark bookkeeping before the second raises `ValueError`; after truncation that high-water mark is past EOF. If no shard existed before the call, the rollback also leaves an empty `.jsonl`, so the state is not "none" as guaranteed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log/_eventlog.py:append_many

chunk_findings.detail: `_held_key` builds the re-entrancy guard key from `str(path)` without canonicalizing the path (`resolve()`/realpath). `flock` is per open-file-description, so a second `os.open` of the same lock file through a different spelling of the path — e.g. `Path("repo/.ddflow/log.lock")` held by thread T, then a nested transaction through `Path("repo/.ddflow/log.lock").resolve()` — produces a different key in `_HELD`. The second acquisition therefore opens the same file again and blocks or times out against the lock T already holds. The guard’s own comment says two EventLog objects for one repo is the exact same-thread re-entry case this key exists to handle, so the key must use a canonical file identity, not the raw path string.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log/_lock.py:_held_key

chunk_findings.detail: `_snapshot_frame` is the validation gate documented to dismiss a malformed frame and degrade to a slower read. It only checks that `tuples` is a `list`, not that each element is a tuple matching `_EVENT_FIELDS`. A malformed frame such as `(10, "abc", 0, [1, 2])` is returned as valid; when the snapshot-seeding code later tries to rebuild `Event` objects from that list, the bad element escapes as a trusted event tuple and can raise instead of being ignored.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log/_parse.py:_snapshot_frame

chunk_findings.detail: `_parser_stamp` claims to fingerprint the code that turns a line into an `Event`, but it hashes only code objects, `co_consts`, and `co_names`. `_recover_glued` depends on the module-global `_LINE_START`; changing that value changes recovery behavior, yet the fingerprint is unchanged because only the name `_LINE_START`, not its bound string value, is hashed. A snapshot written under the old marker can therefore be reused under a parser with different recovery behavior.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log/_parse.py:_parser_stamp

chunk_findings.detail:
The bounded tail reader can silently return `""` even when a final non-empty line exists. With the documented 64 KiB `TAIL_MAX_BYTES`, take a file of size 65537: `b"a
" + b"b"*65535`. At the last loop iteration `window = 65536`, `fh.seek(1)` reads `b"
" + b"b"*65535`; after `split(b"
")` and filtering empty segments, only the final `b` line remains, so `len(lines) > 1` is false and `size <= window` is false (65537 > 65536). The loop exits and returns `""`, despite the final non-empty line being shorter than the bound.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log/_read.py:_last_line

chunk_findings.detail: `_TRAILING_CITE` only captures the *last* trailing bracket group, so a bullet that cites several lessons in separate trailing brackets is treated as citing one. Given a hand-written summary bullet like `- **Cache invalidation.** explanation [L12] [L13]`, `tail.group(1)` is `L13`, so `_summary_bullet` records `cites=["L13"]` instead of `["L12", "L13"]`. `_attach_summaries` then sees exactly one citation and, if lesson `L13` has no summary yet, attaches this bullet as `L13`'s summary instead of importing it as a consolidated rule; the citation to `L12` is lost. This misattributes summary provenance and can suppress the consolidated lesson the importer is supposed to create when a bullet cites more than one lesson.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_scan.py `_summary_bullet`

chunk_findings.detail: The namespace injection only publishes names listed in each submodule's `__all__`; it does not publish the core helpers imported by the package itself (`glob_match`, `_slug`, `_slug_words`). The file's comment says the flat namespace is published into each submodule so functions can call helpers by bare name, and the noqa imports of `_slug`/`_slug_words` indicate they are intended to remain in that flat namespace. Given a submodule function that uses one of these names bare (as the original flat module could), calling it through the package will raise `NameError` because the name is present in the package globals but absent from the submodule's globals; the `globals().update(_EXPORTS)` call does not inject it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/__init__.py:40

chunk_findings.detail: With `[dedupe] on_match = "warn"`, `_resolve_chains` is called unconditionally on the `dropped` map even though no duplicate is actually left out in warn mode. If a summary lesson `A` duplicates a non-summary lesson `B` from the same import (`where="import"`, score 1.0), and `B` duplicates an existing queue record `C` (`where="queue"`, score 0.8), `_resolve_chains` rewrites `A`'s duplicate to point at `C` (`of="C"`, `where="queue"`, `identical=False`, `score=0.8`). Since warn mode keeps `B` in `plan.found`, `A` should still be reported as duplicating `B` in this import; the code instead hides the exact in-import duplicate and reports a transitive `A ~ C` relation that `similar.screen` never established. This violates the function's own contract that a chain is resolved only when the intermediate record "is itself left out."
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_apply.py:_dedupe_found

chunk_findings.detail: `_triage_found` builds `closed` by appending `Found` objects (`closed.append(f)`), but `_note_withheld` is written for `closed: list[str]` and renders it with `', '.join(closed[:_NOTE_EXAMPLES])`. Given a source file that yields a closed/declined open task and `include_done=False`, `_triage_found` returns that item as a `Found` in `closed`; when the plan_import path passes the returned `closed` to `_note_withheld`, `str.join` raises `TypeError: sequence item 0: expected str instance, Found found`. The comment in `_note_withheld` explicitly says closed items should be named like held ones, so `_triage_found` should append an id/title string, not the `Found`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_phases.py:_note_withheld / _triage_found

chunk_findings.detail: Uniquifying against only `proposed` before checking `known` makes already-imported handling order-dependent. Suppose the queue already contains item id `L-x` from a prior import, and this scan contains two items whose scanner-derived id is also `L-x`: a new item first, then the already-imported item. The new item gets `L-x` from `_unique`, then the `f.ident in known` test treats it as the existing item and skips it. The already-imported item then gets uniquified to `L-x-2`, is no longer seen as known, and is appended to `plan.found`, duplicating the existing `L-x` item on re-run. If the second item has `legacy_ident=L-x`, it is instead skipped under the wrong suffixed id and the new item is never imported. `existing_phases` and `plan.skipped_existing` also receive the suffixed id, so phase settle later cannot match the queue item.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_phases.py:_triage_found

chunk_findings.detail: `_note_sources` strips the source string at the first colon before testing for the `git:` scheme: `rel = str(n["source"]).split(":", 1)[0]`, then `if rel and not rel.startswith("git:")`. For a note whose source is `git:feature-branch`, `rel` is `git`, and `"git".startswith("git:")` is false, so the function adds the path `git` to `paths`. `verify_import` later stats `repo / "git"`; in a normal repository with no regular file named `git`, it reports that imported note as having a vanished source. The intended exclusion of branch/git provenance never happens.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_plan.py:_note_sources

chunk_findings.detail: The empty-phase removal only treats phases as live when they are referenced by items already in `plan.found`: `live_phases` is built from `plan.found` tasks and `plan.found` needs. It ignores already-existing open queue items. If the folded queue contains an open task `T` whose `needs` includes phase id `P`, and this import proposes phase `P` but no tasks under `P` (for example, `T` was queued separately and only the phase is missing), `P` is classified as an empty phase and removed. The import then leaves `T` depending on an unknown phase, which is treated as unmet, while the proposal can report success; this is precisely the failure mode the added `needs` union comment says it was meant to avoid.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_cap_or_settle

chunk_findings.detail: The final “Nothing recognisable was found” note is added whenever `plan.found`, `plan.skipped_existing`, and `plan.duplicates` are all empty, even when items were recognised and deliberately withheld. For example, with a todo file containing one checked box and `include_done=False`, `_triage_found` defers the ticked item, `plan.ticked_left_out` becomes 1, `_note_withheld` records that history was left out, `plan.found` is empty, and the end-of-function condition still appends “Nothing recognisable was found.” The same false note appears after an over-cap refusal or after all phases are dropped as empty: the plan has notes explaining what it found and withheld, but the operator is also told nothing recognisable was found.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_plan.py:plan_import

chunk_findings.detail: When a summary bullet has no explanation after its bold lead, `_summary_text` returns the lead or stray punctuation instead of an empty summary. For input `- **Rule**` (body `**Rule**`) and target title `Rule`, `_LEAD` matches, `rest` is empty, `same` is true, and `return (rest or text) if same else text` returns `**Rule**`, so the lesson's summary duplicates its title. For `- **Rule.**`, the terminal period is not consumed because the separator requires following whitespace, so `rest` is `.` and the summary becomes `.`. This contradicts the function's stated purpose of removing the bold lead when it is the title.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_scan.py:_summary_text

chunk_findings.detail:
The table scanner treats any indented line as a table row because it tests `lines[i].lstrip().startswith("|")`. In Markdown, a line indented four spaces or more is an indented code block, not structure. Given a file containing:

```markdown
    | id | title |
    |----|-------|
    | T1 | Do not import |
```

`fenced[i]` is false (there is no ```/~~~ fence), and the `lstrip()` check accepts all three rows, so `_scan_task_tables` emits a `Found` task for `T1` from what is actually example code.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_tables.py:_scan_task_tables

chunk_findings.detail:
The scanner decides a line is a table header solely from “names id/title and next line is a delimiter”, without checking that the line is the first row of a GFM table. Consecutive pipe rows belong to one table, so a data row can be mistaken for a new header. Given:

```markdown
| name | value |
|------|-------|
| id | title |
|------|-------|
| T1 | Do |
```

a GFM renderer treats this as one table whose header is `name/value`, with `id/title`, `---`, and `T1/Do` as data rows. The code sees the third row as a header followed by a delimiter, sets `cols`, skips the delimiter, and then imports `T1` as a task from the supposed new table.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_tables.py:_scan_task_tables

chunk_findings.detail: `_disposition` returns closed for any checkbox text that merely starts with `~~`, but its own contract says a struck-through item is `~~...~~`. Given the raw item text `~~TODO` (no closing `~~`), the function returns `("closed", "STRUCK THROUGH")` and the live item is disposed as history, even though the tildes are literal/unbalanced rather than Markdown strikethrough.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_tables.py:_disposition

chunk_findings.detail: The negation regex has no word boundary after its short alternatives and places `no` before `nothing`, so it matches the `no` prefix inside ordinary words. In `_prose_needs`, this regex is matched against the text immediately after a dependency keyword. Given `text="Requires node and P2.T1"`, `known={"P2.T1"}`, and `self_id=""`, `_PROSE_NEGATING.match(" node and P2.T1")` succeeds because of the `no` in `node`, so `_prose_needs` returns `[]` instead of `["P2.T1"]`. The same defect defeats the intended `nothing but` exception: `Requires nothing but P2.T1` is also treated as negated and drops the dependency, which can make the importer emit a task without a required dependency and let the queue offer it too early.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_titles.py:_PROSE_NEGATING

chunk_findings.detail: `_box_disposition` cannot return an explicit ACTIVE disposition. The code and comments encode active as an empty first element (`("", "")`), but the function only returns inherited dispositions when `inherited[0]` is truthy. Thus an inherited `**STATUS**: ACTIVE` is treated as “no status.” In an archive file, the next line then applies the archive fallback. For example, in an archived file with heading `## Active work`, line `**STATUS**: ACTIVE`, and checkbox `- [ ] finish feature`, the stack entry is `("", "")`, `inherited[0]` is false, `archived` is true, and the function returns `("hold", "in an archive file ...")`. The task is imported as held despite the section explicitly saying ACTIVE, contradicting the function’s docstring and the stack comment that explicit ACTIVE overrides inheritance.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer/_todo.py:_box_disposition

data.body: Research (RA-policy/RA-consume/D-RA-Q8 in ddflow/services/approvals/policy.py + consume.py + sites.py + config_sections/approvals.py) found the mechanism already exists as STANDING RULES: RULES in policy.py, one per verb, shipped OFF ([approvals].policy=[]), count-capped per item+target by policy_max_uses, each use recorded answered by policy:<id>. But (a) rules have NO TIME WINDOW — only count (policy_max_uses) and a per-ANSWER single-use TTL (approvals.use_ttl_s=3600) — and (b) the GENERIC overnight refusals complete.force and claim.force have NO rule at all (only skip_after_unavailable=gate.skip.failed_review and accept_baseline_red=approve.partial exist), so a tool/reviewer/gate that is honestly 'unavailable' piles up one person-approval per instance through the night. GOAL: a configurable STANDING AUTO-APPROVE WINDOW — the operator pre-authorises the generic T2 class (complete.force, claim.force, gate.skip.failed_review, approve.partial) for the next N hours (default 1h = approvals.standing_window_s 3600, cap 24h = max 86400, configurable per project/--local/env like every knob), every auto-approval recorded as policy:<id> with its digest on approvals log, auto-approval STOPS and a person is asked again the instant the window lapses. NON-GOALS: T3/L4 and non-generic sites stay person-only; the agent identity can never widen it; a rule names one verb, never an arbitrary command. CONFORMANCE r-reuse-core (extend the one RULES table + the one [approvals] config section), r-small-files (<20KB), r-everything-configurable (new knobs with doc+default+override), no behaviour change for callers. Tests first: a pending complete.force files, the standing window answers it as policy:<id> with digest recorded, and a request after the window lapses is NOT auto-approved.
data.title: Standing auto-approve window for generic T2 refusals (default 1h, max 24h, configurable)

data.body: Default rule for ddflow-managed projects: when a gate is recorded skipped (ddflow gate skip ID GATE --reason R), ddflow ALSO auto-files ONE follow-up future task whose scope is ONLY to re-run that gate on that item later. The follow-up is the log entry, the reminder and the effort to RE-RUN the gate, NOT effort to repair the gate-check code nor to do the item payload work. It is dropped when the item is abandoned; completing the item or re-recording the gate non-skipped also settles it. Configurable by company policy / config / user: knob [gates].skip_followup = auto | warn | off, default auto, respecting company-to-project-to-local override; an agent edit of the knob is a config.set needing approval. Extend the ONE gate-record/skip site in ddflow/api/gates.py (the failed-review path is _agent_skip_refusal; the plain skip path is record with skip true / outcome skipped). Reuse the fix_task_followup id-template machinery where reasonable. r-reuse-core, r-small-files, r-everything-configurable, no behaviour change for callers. Tests first: a skip auto-files the follow-up, skip with skip_followup off files none, abandon drops it, re-running the gate and passing settles it.
data.title: Skipped gate auto-files a follow-up task to re-run it later (default-on, configurable, dropped on abandon)

chunk_findings.detail: If a directory contains both a module file `foo.py` and a regular package `foo/__init__.py`, this code selects the file text (`file.is_file()` is true) but then calls `importlib.import_module(f"{__name__}.{name}")`, and Python’s import system prefers the package over the same-named module. For example, if `foo.py` is a helper with no `COMMANDS`/`tool=` text while `foo/__init__.py` declares a valid `COMMANDS` tuple, `_command_modules()` reads only `foo.py`, fails the regex, and silently skips the package, so its commands are never registered. Conversely, a stale/incorrect `foo.py` can cause the package to be imported based on the wrong source text.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/__init__.py:44

chunk_findings.detail: The `exit_code` parameter for `ddflow_gate_record` is declared with `cli_type=int` but without `type="integer"`, unlike the other integer parameters in this file (`gate run --timeout` and `gate skip --exit-code`). If the MCP schema generator derives JSON types from `Param.type`, the tool schema will not constrain `exit_code` to an integer, so a client following the schema can send `"0"`. That value reaches `_api().GateEvidence(exit_code="0")`; any truthiness or `!= 0` check in the API then treats a zero exit code as non-zero/failure, recording a passing command as failed. The parameter should declare `type="integer"` to match its intended integer semantics.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/lifecycle/gates.py:gate record/exit_code

chunk_findings.detail: The `wait` command’s contract tells an agent to “sleep until an item … can be claimed” and exposes `--poll` as “seconds between log checks”; it does not require the caller to release any lease it already holds. For example, after `ddflow claim X` (so the agent holds a live lease on `X`), an agent can run `ddflow_wait --item Y --poll 1` and then sleep/poll the log every second while still holding `X`. That is poll-waiting and holding while waiting, contrary to [r-lock-cycle-selfheal], which says agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting and that ddflow should heal blocking by adding needs edges instead.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/lifecycle/navigate.py:wait

chunk_findings.detail: The `block` command is defined without a `summary`, unlike every other command in this file. The declared surface uses `summary` as the one-line description for `ddflow_block`, so `ddflow help block` / the generated tool schema has no short summary; if `Command.summary` is required by the command dataclass, importing this new module raises `TypeError` immediately.

chunk_findings.detail: If a directory contains both a module file `foo.py` and a regular package `foo/__init__.py`, this code selects the file text (`file.is_file()` is true) but then calls `importlib.import_module(f"{__name__}.{name}")`, and Python’s import system prefers the package over the same-named module. For example, if `foo.py` is a helper with no `COMMANDS`/`tool=` text while `foo/__init__.py` declares a valid `COMMANDS` tuple, `_command_modules()` reads only `foo.py`, fails the regex, and silently skips the package, so its commands are never registered. Conversely, a stale/incorrect `foo.py` can cause the package to be imported based on the wrong source text.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/__init__.py:44

chunk_findings.detail: The `exit_code` parameter for `ddflow_gate_record` is declared with `cli_type=int` but without `type="integer"`, unlike the other integer parameters in this file (`gate run --timeout` and `gate skip --exit-code`). If the MCP schema generator derives JSON types from `Param.type`, the tool schema will not constrain `exit_code` to an integer, so a client following the schema can send `"0"`. That value reaches `_api().GateEvidence(exit_code="0")`; any truthiness or `!= 0` check in the API then treats a zero exit code as non-zero/failure, recording a passing command as failed. The parameter should declare `type="integer"` to match its intended integer semantics.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/lifecycle/gates.py:gate record/exit_code

chunk_findings.detail: The `wait` command’s contract tells an agent to “sleep until an item … can be claimed” and exposes `--poll` as “seconds between log checks”; it does not require the caller to release any lease it already holds. For example, after `ddflow claim X` (so the agent holds a live lease on `X`), an agent can run `ddflow_wait --item Y --poll 1` and then sleep/poll the log every second while still holding `X`. That is poll-waiting and holding while waiting, contrary to [r-lock-cycle-selfheal], which says agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting and that ddflow should heal blocking by adding needs edges instead.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/lifecycle/navigate.py:wait

chunk_findings.detail: The `block` command is defined without a `summary`, unlike every other command in this file. The declared surface uses `summary` as the one-line description for `ddflow_block`, so `ddflow help block` / the generated tool schema has no short summary; if `Command.summary` is required by the command dataclass, importing this new module raises `TypeError` immediately.

chunk_findings.detail: The moved `update` treats a `O.nothing` result from `_landed_paths_fields` as a fatal outcome, so a no-op `--landed-paths` request aborts the whole edit even when other fields were valid and planned. For example, given an item whose `landed_paths` is already `["a"]`, calling `update(..., ItemEdit(title="new", landed_paths=["a"]))` makes `plan_edit` return `{"title": "new"}`, but `_landed_paths_fields` sees `paths == it.landed_paths` and returns `O.nothing(...)`; `update` then returns that outcome before `_record_update`, so the title is not changed. The same happens when `landed_paths=[]` is passed to “clear” a restriction that does not exist while other fields are also being updated.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:update

chunk_findings.detail: The package makes `_load` and `DEFAULT_PRIORITY` plain attributes of `ddflow.api.items`, but the actual functions are defined in submodules. If a test first imports a public function, e.g. `from ddflow.api.items import update`, the lazy `__getattr__` imports `_edit` at that time. If `_edit` obtains `_load`/`DEFAULT_PRIORITY` by normal static import from the package or from `.._base`, those names are bound into `_edit`'s module globals. A later `monkeypatch.setattr(items, "_load", fake)` or `monkeypatch.setattr(items, "DEFAULT_PRIORITY", fake)` changes only the package namespace, not the already-imported submodule's globals, so `update`/`task_add` still call the original `_load`/priority. In the old single module, the function's globals were the package/module globals, so patching `items._load` was observed at call time. This breaks the monkeypatch behavior the docstring explicitly promises.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/__init__.py:18-33

chunk_findings.detail: The body of `_add_ports` is malformed: `pid = f"{item}@{ln}" IT.add_task(` is not valid Python because two expressions are juxtaposed with no operator, separator, or assignment target. Importing this module/package will raise `SyntaxError` at parse time. Even if the line were repaired by inserting a newline/semicolon, the shown loop then passes `port` to `IT.add_task` and checks `added.ok`, but neither `port` nor `added` is assigned in the shown code; the expected `port = replace(...)` and `added = IT.add_task(...)` assignments are missing. Any import of `ddflow.api.items` that reaches this submodule fails.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_add.py:140 (`_add_ports`)

chunk_findings.detail: The generated-port clash check ignores `readd` and treats removed tombstones as existing. The state clearly includes removed items: `_port_of_lines` checks `origin.removed` and filters `not o.removed` from `st.items.values()`. Therefore, if a previous multi-line task created port `X@release` and that port was removed, a later call such as `task_add(repo, "X", lines="main,release", readd=True)` (with `X` itself absent or removed so the main `IT.taken(..., readd=True)` check passes) reaches line 248, sees `f"{item}@{ln}" in st.items` as true for `X@release`, and returns failed `"X@release already exist"`. This contradicts the documented behavior that `readd` lets a removed id come back, and it also contradicts the later call to `_add_ports(..., readd=readd)`, which indicates generated ports should honor `readd`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_add.py:248 (`task_add`)

chunk_findings.detail: The `_line_frozen` body contains a malformed line: `ports = [o.id for o in st.items.values() if o.port_from ==terminal or it.lease:` is not valid Python (unclosed list comprehension and a colon after an assignment). As written, importing `ddflow/api/items/_edit.py` raises `SyntaxError`, so `update`, `plan_edit`, and everything re-exported through the new package fail before any item can be updated.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:_line_frozen

chunk_findings.detail: `_landed_paths_fields` returns `O.nothing` when the requested `landed_paths` are already the current restriction, or when clearing an already-empty restriction, and `update` returns that outcome unconditionally even when other fields were planned. For example, on an item with no existing `landed_paths`, calling `update(repo, id, ItemEdit(title="new", landed_paths=[]))` puts `title` into `fields`, then `_landed_paths_fields` sees no restriction to clear, returns `O.nothing`, and `update` returns before `_record_update`, so the title change is silently dropped. The same happens with `ItemEdit(title="new", landed_paths=current_paths)`; an unchanged `--landed-paths` argument should not veto other requested edits.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:update

chunk_findings.detail: The split drafts do not propagate the parent item's dependencies, and the `needs` argument is applied only to the first part. For an item `A` that already needs `X`, `split(A, into=["B", "C"])` creates `B` and `C` with `needs=[]` (unless the caller also passes `needs`, in which case only `B` gets it and `C` still needs nothing). Those children are the work that replaces `A`, but they can be claimed before `X` is done, so the parent's dependency constraint is lost even though `globs` and `priority` are inherited.
