chunk_findings.detail: If a command family exists both as a module file and as a package directory with the same name, the scan reads the wrong source. The new `names` set collapses `foo.py` and `foo/__init__.py` to one name `foo`, and `file.is_file()` makes the code read only `foo.py`; the later `importlib.import_module(f"{__name__}.{name}")` imports the package, because Python gives packages priority over same-named modules. For example, if `ddflow/surfaces/declared/foo.py` is a helper with no `COMMANDS` and `ddflow/surfaces/declared/foo/__init__.py` declares a valid `COMMANDS` tuple/list, the loop reads `foo.py`, fails `_HAS_COMMANDS`, and never imports or registers the package. Thus the package support can silently drop commands whenever a same-named module file is present.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/__init__.py:36-43

chunk_findings.detail: The `gate skip` command calls `_api().gate_record(...)` but does not request or forward `called_from`, while the sibling `gate record` command sets `wants_called_from=True` and passes that argument. Given an MCP call to `ddflow_gate_skip(id="item", gate="review", reason="...")`, the lambda has no `called_from` parameter, so the recorded skip event is written without the source-surface context that ordinary gate records receive. This defeats the audit trail for a recorded override (and, if `gate_record` expects `called_from` to distinguish CLI vs MCP/unknown callers, can cause a TypeError or misattributed event).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/lifecycle/gates.py:gate skip call

chunk_findings.detail: The new `wait` command makes waiting/polling a first-class agent operation: its `call` blocks until an item or lease can be claimed, and it exposes a `poll` parameter (“Seconds between log checks”) with no minimum enforced here. For example, after a claim is refused because another agent holds the item, an agent can call `ddflow_wait(item="T1", timeout=300, poll=2)` (or CLI `--poll 2`), causing the agent to hold while waiting/poll logs instead of ddflow healing the dependency/circular wait. This violates [r-lock-cycle-selfheal], which says agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting and ddflow should heal undetected circular waits by adding needs edges.

chunk_findings.detail: The re-export mechanism only makes the package attribute resolve to the submodule object on first access. It does not propagate rebinding of private helpers back into the submodule globals where the public functions look them up. Concretely, existing callers/tests that do `monkeypatch.setattr(ddflow.core.redact, "_marker", fake)` and then call `ddflow.core.redact.redact_text(...)` used to see `fake` in the old single-module `ddflow.core.redact` globals; in the split package, `redact_text` runs in `ddflow.core.redact.engine` and resolves `_marker` from `engine`’s globals, which the package-level assignment did not change. This breaks the stated no-behavior-change and the docstring’s “monkeypatch … exactly as before” invariant for these patch-covered private names.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/__init__.py:73

chunk_findings.detail: `repo_root` with a trailing slash prevents the repo-root path redaction from matching normal rooted paths. The regex is `re.compile(re.escape(root) + r"(?![\w.-])")`; for `redact_text("[REDACTED:path]", secret_patterns=[], repo_root="[REDACTED:path]")`, the regex consumes `[REDACTED:path]` and then the lookahead sees `f`, which is in `[\w]`, so the match fails. The root is not redacted as a path even though the function contract says `repo_root` is removed, leaking the repository root path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/engine.py:redact_text

chunk_findings.detail: The mask fallback leakes the first token of a two-token matched secret. `mask_secrets("hunter2 swordfish", ["hunter2 swordfish"])` matches the full string; `_mask` reaches `parts = s.split(None, 1)` and returns `f"{parts[0]} [REDACTED]"`, `hunter2 [REDACTED]`. Because the caller declared the entire matched text a secret, preserving the first half of the secret is an under-redaction leak. It should return `[REDACTED]` unless the first token is recognized as a key/context.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/engine.py:_mask

chunk_findings.detail: The idempotence guard only skips matches that are exactly a full `_MARKER` (`_MARKER.fullmatch(m.group(0))`), while `whole=True` scans through markers. Given `redact_text("[REDACTED:secret]", secret_patterns=[r"REDACTED"])`, the pattern matches `REDACTED` inside the marker and replaces it with `[REDACTED:secret]`, yielding `[[REDACTED:secret]:secret]`. This corrupts already-redacted text and violates the module's promise that a marker is never scanned again.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/engine.py:_secrets

chunk_findings.detail: Given input `kind="bug.fixed"` and `data={"item": "bug_2026-10-15_01", "lesson": "..."}`, `redact_event_data` redacts the `item` id. `"item"` is not in `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS["bug.fixed"]` (`"lesson", "changelog", "regression_verify"`), is not in `LOG_VERBATIM_NAMES`, and `("bug.fixed", "item")` is absent from `LOG_VERBATIM_FIELDS`, so the function falls into the `else` branch and replaces the item id with a redaction marker. Since other bug-lifecycle payloads that reference an item explicitly preserve it (for example `("bug.found", "item")` is in `LOG_VERBATIM_FIELDS`), `bug.fixed` item ids should also be preserved; the committed `bug.fixed` event data is corrupted.

chunk_findings.detail: The new knobs are documented as bounding the generic T2 class (`complete.force`, `claim.force`, `gate.skip.failed_review`, `approve.partial`), but `standing_verbs` is explicitly scoped only to the two new windowed rules (`complete_unavailable`, `claim_unavailable`) while the existing `skip_after_unavailable` and `accept_baseline_red` rules “fire as before.” Given `[approvals].policy = ["skip_after_unavailable", "accept_baseline_red"]`, any `standing_window_s` (for example the default 3600), and satisfied rule conditions, a `gate.skip.failed_review` or `approve.partial` request is still auto-approved after the standing window has lapsed—indeed even if `standing_verbs` is cleared—because those rules ignore the window. This contradicts the stated “auto-approval stops the instant the window lapses” behavior for the generic T2 class and makes the default `standing_verbs` list, which includes those verbs, misleading.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/approvals.py:standing_window_s/standing_verbs

chunk_findings.detail: The standing window is enforced only for rules whose `windowed` field is true. The existing generic T2 rules `skip_after_unavailable` (`gate.skip.failed_review`) and `accept_baseline_red` (`approve.partial`) remain `windowed=False`, and the new comment explicitly says they “fire whenever switched on.” Thus, if an operator enables `[approvals].policy=["skip_after_unavailable", "accept_baseline_red", "complete_unavailable", "claim_unavailable"]` with `standing_window_s=3600` and `standing_verbs` containing all four generic T2 verbs, `complete.force` and `claim.force` will stop auto-approving after the window lapses, but `gate.skip.failed_review` and `approve.partial` will continue to auto-approve indefinitely (subject only to the per-subject `policy_max_uses` cap). This defeats the stated goal that the generic T2 class is pre-authorised only for the configured window and that auto-approval stops when the window lapses.
chunk_findings.title: policy.py:RULES / _window_open

chunk_findings.detail: The window anchor is inferred from the `answered_at` values of windowed policy answers in `asks_of(state)`, but those answered asks are subject to `approvals.use_ttl_s` (default 3600) according to the change context. When `standing_window_s` is longer than the answer TTL, the anchor can disappear or be superseded by a later answer before the configured window has expired. For example, with `standing_window_s=86400` and `use_ttl_s=3600`, a complete.force auto-approved at t=0 is no longer present after t=3600; if another windowed auto-approval occurs at t=86399, `window_start` returns 86399, so at t=86401 `_window_open` still returns True and auto-approves, even though the original 24-hour window from t=0 lapsed at t=86400. This lets the standing window roll forward beyond the configured maximum as long as windowed answers keep appearing within the answer TTL. The window start/expiry should be persisted independently of TTL-bound answered asks.
chunk_findings.title: policy.py:window_start

chunk_findings.detail: The new window tests never make a second `operator_gate` call while the window is known to be open. The first test only makes the call that opens the window; the lapse test makes one call to open it, advances past expiry, then makes a second call expected to be denied. Therefore an implementation that records a `window_start` on the first policy approval but never uses that open window to answer later requests (or that answers only the request that opens the window) still passes all three new tests: the opening request is `ok` with `via=policy`, `window_start > 0.0`, the post-expiry request is denied, and the out-of-scope first request is denied. That does not demonstrate the stated goal that the standing window auto-approves subsequent generic T2 refusals for the next N hours; a request before the expiry must also be asserted `ok` with a policy stamp.

The window start/expiry should be persisted independently of TTL-bound answered asks.
chunk_findings.title: policy.py:window_start

chunk_findings.detail: The new window tests never make a second `operator_gate` call while the window is known to be open. The first test only makes the call that opens the window; the lapse test makes one call to open it, advances past expiry, then makes a second call expected to be denied. Therefore an implementation that records a `window_start` on the first policy approval but never uses that open window to answer later requests (or that answers only the request that opens the window) still passes all three new tests: the opening request is `ok` with `via=policy`, `window_start > 0.0`, the post-expiry request is denied, and the out-of-scope first request is denied. That does not demonstrate the stated goal that the standing window auto-approves subsequent generic T2 refusals for the next N hours; a request before the expiry must also be asserted `ok` with a policy stamp.

chunk_findings.detail: `window_start` computes the standing-window anchor from every ask row with a non-empty `policy` field, without restricting that set to rules currently enabled in `[approvals].policy` or to rows whose verb is in `[approvals].standing_verbs`. Thus an old policy answer from a disabled, removed, or out-of-scope rule controls `_window_open`. For example, if `skip_after_unavailable` auto-approved at `t=0` and was later disabled, then enabling `complete_unavailable` with `standing_verbs=["complete.force"]` and `standing_window_s=3600` sees `window_start() == 0.0` for the first `complete.force` at `t=7200`, so `_window_open` returns false and the request is person-only even though no in-scope standing rule has fired. Conversely, if the disabled rule fired at `t=7000`, the first `complete.force` at `t=7100` is auto-approved and the window closes at `t=10600`, 3600 seconds after the unrelated old answer rather than after the first complete-force standing approval. This violates the stated behavior that the first in-scope standing auto-approval opens the full configured window.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/policy.py:window_start

chunk_findings.detail: The test advances the clock by `cfg.approvals.standing_window_s + 1`, but the documented defaults make `standing_window_s` and the pre-existing `approvals.use_ttl_s` both 3600. Thus the assertion can pass for the wrong reason: if `operator_gate` persists `window_start` (so the first test passes) but still decides expiry only from the old per-answer TTL/count logic, then after 3601 seconds the TTL has also lapsed and `not after.ok` is true even though the new standing-window check is absent or inert. The test should set the two durations apart (for example `standing_window_s=60`, `use_ttl_s=3600`) and advance only past the window to prove the window, not the TTL, is what stops auto-approval.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_approvals_policy.py:test_a_windowed_rule_stops_the_instant_the_window_lapses_and_a_person_is_asked

chunk_findings.detail: The test reuses the same `canon` after the window lapses and only asserts `after.ask_id` and `"requested" in after.message`. It never captures the first auto-approved ask id or asserts that `after.ask_id` is a new, unanswered ask. If `operator_gate` returns the already answered ask id from the first policy approval together with its original “approval requested” message, the test still passes even though no new person ask was created, so it does not actually refute a stale-ask false positive.

chunk_findings.detail: When an `update` changes some fields but the `landed_paths` value is a no-op, the code returns the landed-paths outcome and discards the other requested changes. For example, given item `X` that already has `landed_paths=["a.py"]` and `globs=["a.py"]`, call `update(repo, "X", ItemEdit(globs=["b.py"], landed_paths=["a.py"]))` (CLI equivalent: `ddflow update X --globs b.py --landed-paths a.py`). `plan_edit` correctly returns `{"globs": ["b.py"]}`; `update` then calls `_landed_paths_fields`, which sees `paths == it.landed_paths` and returns `O.nothing(... already restricts ...)`. Because `update` returns immediately on any `O.Outcome` from `_landed_paths_fields`, the `globs` edit is never recorded, even though it was valid and requested. The same abort also happens for a no-op clear (`--landed-paths ""` when no restriction exists) and can prevent a `--worktree` rebind requested in the same edit.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:update / _landed_paths_fields

chunk_findings.detail: The new submodule does `from ddflow.api import items as _items` while it is itself part of `ddflow.api.items`. Because the new `__init__.py` re-exports the public API by importing this module, this line runs during initialization of `ddflow.api.items`, before the parent package `ddflow.api` has an `items` attribute set. The first `import ddflow.api.items` or `from ddflow.api.items import task_add` therefore raises `ImportError: cannot import name 'items' from partially initialized module 'ddflow.api'`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_add.py:9

chunk_findings.detail: The multi-line clash check ignores `readd` and removed items: `clash = [f"{item}@{ln}" for ln in wanted if f"{item}@{ln}" in st.items]`. Given an existing removed port `T@dev`, calling `task_add(repo, "T", lines="main,dev", readd=True)` fails with `T@dev already exist`, because `st.items` contains removed items (the same file relies on this in `_port_of_lines` when it tests `origin.removed`). This contradicts the documented `readd` behavior that a removed id may come back; `_add_ports` would pass `readd` to `IT.add_task`, but the premature clash check returns before that happens.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_add.py:task_add

chunk_findings.detail: `plan_edit` treats a no-op add/remove fold as “nothing to change” even when `edit.worktree` is set. `_nothing_to_change` only inspects the `needs`/`tags`/`globs` folds, and `update` only ignores a `NOTHING` outcome from `plan_edit` when `edit.landed` or `edit.landed_paths` is present. Given an item whose tags already include `bug`, `update(repo, id, ItemEdit(add_tags=["bug"], worktree="/linked/wt"))` folds `tags` back to the current list, `_nothing_to_change` returns a “nothing to change” message, `plan_edit` returns `O.nothing`, and `update` returns that outcome without calling `_update_and_rebind`; the requested `--worktree` rebind is silently skipped. The same path also bypasses the intended empty-worktree refusal for `worktree=""` when combined with a no-op fold.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:plan_edit/_nothing_to_change

chunk_findings.detail: `update` aborts on any outcome returned by `_landed_paths_fields`, including `O.nothing`, even when other fields are set. Given an item with a landed range and `landed_paths=["a.py"]`, `update(repo, id, ItemEdit(title="New", landed_paths=["a.py"]))` makes `_landed_paths_fields` return `O.nothing` because the restriction is unchanged; `update` returns that immediately, so the title is not recorded. Likewise, `ItemEdit(landed_paths=[])` on an item with no path restriction returns nothing and discards any other fields or a `worktree` rebind. A redundant or no-op path-restriction edit should not suppress the rest of the update.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:update

chunk_findings.detail: `_refile_problem` validates each proposed new id against the current state with `IT.taken(st, nid, readd=False)`, but it never checks that the proposed ids are distinct from each other. For a contested item with two losing definitions, a call such as `resolve(..., keep=..., refile_as="new1,new1")` passes validation: both occurrences of `new1` are seen as unused in the pre-transaction `st`. `_apply_resolution` then zips `new_ids` with the two lost definitions and appends two `{family}.added` events for the same id `new1`, creating duplicate item ids / a bogus refiled contest instead of refusing the invalid input.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_resolve.py:_refile_problem

chunk_findings.detail: This module is a submodule of the package it imports at top level. The package `ddflow/api/items/__init__.py` is described as re-exporting the public API, so it must import this module to expose `split`. When that happens, `ddflow.api.items` is already in `sys.modules` but has not yet been set as an attribute on `ddflow.api`; the top-level `from ddflow.api import items as _items` therefore executes during initialization and raises an ImportError for a partially initialized module. Using `_items._load` only inside functions does not save it, because the import statement itself fails.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_split.py:7

chunk_findings.detail: `needs` is applied only to the first child (`needs=csv_list(needs) if i == 1 else []`). Given `split(repo, A, into=["B", "C"], needs="X")`, child `B` depends on `X` but child `C` has no needs. If `A` was blocked by `X`, or if the caller expected the supplied `needs` to apply to every split part, `C` can be claimed before `X` completes, bypassing the dependency. The parent’s own needs are also never copied to any child, so splitting a blocked item can make its sub-tasks unblocked.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_split.py:118

chunk_findings.detail: `_fail_fast("pytest -xq")` returns False because `shlex.split` leaves combined pytest short options as the single token `-xq`, which is not detected by `t in ("-x", "--exitfirst")`. In `_rerun_failed_tests`, that makes the fail-fast guard false for a rerun that actually stopped at the first failure, so tests after the first are wrongly marked as `flaked` and written to the flake log even though the rerun never ran them.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates/_run.py:_fail_fast

chunk_findings.detail: When `cwd` was removed by `merge` while the gate was still running, the function sets `asked = cwd if cwd.is_dir() else repo` so ancestry checks use the repository, but the subsequent `for newer, what in ((G.tree_identity(cwd), ...), ...)` still calls `G.tree_identity(cwd)` on the now-missing directory. The git call therefore fails and raises out of `_execute` instead of reaching `G.superseded_by(..., asked, ...)` and returning the documented “could not tell keeps the record” result.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates/_run.py:_superseded_run

chunk_findings.detail: An ordinary `ddflow ci run` command with no `--timeout`, no bare `--`, and no quoted/backslash text makes `_CI_WORDS.finditer(command)` yield no matches. The `for ... else` block then executes with `m` unbound and raises `UnboundLocalError`. For example, `_with_run_timeout(cfg, gdef, 60, "item", "gate")` with `gdef.command == "ddflow ci run pytest"` passes the `_CI_VERB.match` guard but crashes instead of returning `ddflow ci run --timeout 60 pytest`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates/_timeout.py:_ci_command_with_timeout

chunk_findings.detail: When the command contains an old `--timeout` and no later bare `--`, the tail is rebuilt starting at `m.start()` before the old option, not after it, so the old option remains in the result. `_ci_command_with_timeout("ddflow ci run --timeout 5 echo hi", 60)` returns `"ddflow ci run --timeout 60 --timeout 5 echo hi"` instead of `"ddflow ci run --timeout 60 echo hi"`, so the timeout override does not actually replace the CI budget and can make the command invalid or use the old value.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates/_timeout.py:_ci_command_with_timeout

chunk_findings.detail: The first branch `if it.worktree:` honors a stored worktree without checking `cfg.worktree.enabled`. Given an item that already has a worktree and `[worktree].enabled` is later set to `false` (the lone-agent switch), and the item has not merged, `item_tree` returns that linked worktree instead of the primary. This contradicts the function's own contract that with worktrees off the primary stays the answer, and a worktree-gated run will execute in the stale linked worktree.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates/_tree.py:item_tree

chunk_findings.detail: `_evidence_fields` uses `if evidence.ci_scope:` to decide whether to record the caller-supplied CI scope. `ci_scope` is typed `dict[str, Any] | None`, so an empty dict `{}` is a valid provided value meaning “the `ci run` selected no tests,” but it is falsy and is not recorded in `ev`. Given input `Evidence(ci_scope={})`, the event loses the fact that a CI scope was supplied; downstream cannot distinguish that from “no `ci_scope` provided.” It should use `if evidence.ci_scope is not None:`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates/_vet.py:_evidence_fields

chunk_findings.detail: The package re-exports patch-covered private names such as `_mask`, `_marker`, `_coerce`, and `_secrets` from submodules, but assigning to `ddflow.core.redact._mask` only sets that name in `ddflow.core.redact.__dict__`. Functions such as `redact_text` resolve `_mask` from `ddflow.core.redact.engine`'s module globals, not from the package globals, so the patch is ignored. Previously both the function and the patched private lived in `ddflow.core.redact`'s single module namespace, so `unittest.mock.patch("ddflow.core.redact._mask", fake)` would change `redact_text` behavior. This contradicts the docstring's claim that monkeypatching still "re-binds the name on THIS module exactly as before."
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/__init__.py:_SUBMODULE_OF

chunk_findings.detail: `_secrets` runs the user regex over the whole text (`whole=True`), but `settled` only keeps a match when the entire match equals a marker. A valid pattern that matches text inside a produced marker breaks idempotence: `redact_text("secret", secret_patterns=[r"secret"])` first returns `[REDACTED:secret]`; a second identical call matches the `secret` suffix inside that marker and returns `[REDACTED:[REDACTED:secret]]`. This violates the pass's documented idempotence and corrupts already-redacted output.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/engine.py:_secrets.settled

chunk_findings.detail: `_mask` treats any two blank-delimited words as `key value` and returns `f"{parts[0]} [REDACTED]"`. When a caller supplies a pattern that matches an actual multi-word secret, this leaks the first word: `mask_secrets("hunter2 launch", [r"hunter2 launch"])` returns `"hunter2 [REDACTED]"`, leaving part of the secret visible. Since `_secrets` accepts arbitrary regexes, this can defeat redaction for phrase-style secrets.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/engine.py:_mask

chunk_findings.detail: `("job.started", "cwd")` is classified as `LOG_VERBATIM_FIELDS`, so `redact_event_data` keeps that field with only `redact_network` applied. Given input `redact_event_data("job.started", {"cwd": "[REDACTED:path]"}, redactor, lookup_network=True)`, the returned dict still contains `"cwd": "[REDACTED:path]"` because `redact_network` masks private IPs/hostnames, not filesystem paths. That commits a home path unredacted even though this same module explicitly redacts `session.started.cwd` in `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS` and documents that a home path must never be committed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/log.py:LOG_VERBATIM_FIELDS / redact_event_data

chunk_findings.detail: `_loop` calls `_parse(m.group(1), ip_type).is_loopback` without the `try/except ValueError` guard that `_is_private` uses. `_IPV4` is only a syntactic pattern, so it legitimately matches invalid dotted quads such as `999.1.1.1`; `_loop(_IPV4.search("999.1.1.1"), ipaddress.IPv4Address)` raises `ipaddress.AddressValueError` instead of returning `False`. Any caller that iterates `_IPV4`/`_IPV6` matches and passes them to `_loop` will crash on that ordinary input.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/pattern.py:_loop

chunk_findings.detail: After `python -m` is processed, `leading` is left `False`, and the special case that appends the wrapped program (`elif tok in _PROGRAMS and out[-1] == "-m":`) does not restore `leading = True`. For `redact_argv(["python", "-m", "ddflow", "view"], subcommands=["view"])`, the result is `["python", "-m", "ddflow", "<arg>"]`, but `view` is an allowed leading subcommand and should be kept according to the function’s own docstring. The special case needs to reset the leading context once it has recognized `ddflow`/`ddflow-mcp` as the real program after Python’s `-m`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact/profiles.py:redact_argv

data.claim: The split-lane contention is two shared single-lease files whose per-split edits are pure re-homes of derivable data: constants-exemptions.toml keys are file:name paths, and ARCHITECTURE.md module tokens are file paths. The constants loader already merges per-module fragments (constants-exemptions.d/*.toml), so the register can live per-module and a split lane re-homes only its own module file.
data.falsifier: A .d fragment would NOT merge into the register (load_register ignored it), so a per-module fragment could not register a constant and the ratchet would still demand the shared file.
data.mechanism: constants_audit.load_register reads [REGISTER, *glob(FRAGMENTS)], so splitting the register into per-module fragments does not change the merged register the ratchet (tests/test_constants_ratchet.py) audits.

data.claim: The gate-failed reason is derived from the single 'best' reviewer only, so a blocking finding raised by a different reviewer leaves the reason empty and record() raises.
data.falsifier: A single reviewer raising a finding would crash the same way (it does not: _reason_of(best) then returns 'N finding(s)').
data.mechanism: _gate_outcome blocks on found aggregated across every REVIEWED reviewer, but _record_review builds the reason from _reason_of(best); best=min(status) picks the first fully-reviewed reviewer, which may have no findings while another reviewer raised one.
data.probe: Repro with two command reviewers (clean + finder): first round clean (pass), a fix commit adds a FINDME line the 'finder' reviewer flags; the delta re-review records best=clean with no findings but blocks on finder's finding.

data.claim: The default ddflow pipeline has no pass that scans a self-assessment text and files its named defects; r-ddflow-self-assessment is advisory only, so filing depends on per-agent compliance. Adding a defensive pass with an off-able knob makes the filing default.

data.mechanism: A [self_assessment].auto_file knob (default true) gates ddflow.api.knowledge.self_assessment.auto_file, wired at session end, phase end, pre-compaction and any assessment text; each named defect is filed via bug found --scope ddflow (--no-task when the fix ships in the finding commit) and one reading like an existing record is skipped.

data.body: The slash command /ddflow-wave loads ddflow-orchestrator as a PRIMARY agent (agent: ddflow-orchestrator, no subtask flag) and the agent file is mode: all with instruction 1 wrapping the mission in ONE foreground session goal (goal start). Result: the main Kilo session blocks while the orchestrator runs, and async notifications from its task subagents only surface after the user presses ctrl+b to background it. Fix with two one-line edits: (1) .kilo/command/ddflow-wave.md YAML frontmatter add a line subtask: true so the command runs as a background subtask; (2) .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md change mode: all to mode: subagent so the orchestrator only runs via the Task tool (background), never as a primary agent. Preserve everything else. This is a docs/config housekeeping commit (the .kilo driver files); commit under the task lease.
data.title: Run ddflow-wave orchestrator as a background subtask, not a foreground goal

data.body: The ddflow wave-orchestrator (read ddflow next ready set, fan each ready item to a task subagent by tier, re-read next after each merge/park, wait via background processes and ddflow wait, persist the wave position in memory, stop ONLY on a question or operator gate) is today hand-written per harness: Kilo ships .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md + .kilo/command/ddflow-wave.md, while claude-code/opencode/vscode keep prose driver deltas under docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/. The loop is harness-agnostic and should be DATA (one spec) emitted to each harness, like the rest of P-drivers 'drivers as data'. Generalize into a driver ORCHESTRATION record (the wave loop, subagent fanout tiers, wait/re-read, position persistence, stop-only-on-question) that each harness driver instantiates (Kilo session goal + task subagent, Claude Code Task, opencode subtask, vscode). Deliverable: replace the hand-written .kilo orchestrator files with emitted copies and add the orchestration section to the claude-code/opencode/vscode/kilo-cline deltas. Note: this is a P-drivers item (harness/runtime as data); the 'adapter' is a per-harness DRIVER, not a P-adapters external-dependency port.
data.title: Orchestration wave-driver as data: one harness-agnostic loop spec emitted per harness
